name: reference_mac_app_logging_and_log_shadowing
description: "A zsh function named `log` shadows /usr/bin/log and makes every `log show` return nothing — plus how Owletto's Mac app logging actually works (Log.swift, ~/Library/Logs/Owletto, LOBU_OWLETTO_LOG_DIR)"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: 259b2997-9a73-4761-987d-67f0a02cf9fe
---

## The trap: `log` is shadowed in this shell

There is a zsh function named `log` on this machine. Every `log show …` invocation
hits it, not `/usr/bin/log`, and it fails with:

    (eval):log:1: too many arguments

With `2>/dev/null` on the command — which is the natural thing to write — this
looks like **an empty result set**, not an error. It cost a wrong conclusion
("the Mac app emits no logs at all") that survived three separate predicates and
got as far as being reported to the user. There were 79,897 lines.

**Always use `/usr/bin/log show`, and never suppress stderr on a diagnostic
command whose empty output you intend to reason from.** An absence you can't
distinguish from an error is not evidence — same family as
[[feedback_absence_needs_origin_main_grep]].

Useful predicates once you're calling the real binary:

    /usr/bin/log show --last 3h --predicate 'process == "Owletto"' --style compact
    /usr/bin/log show --last 3h --predicate 'subsystem == "ai.lobu.mac"' --info --debug

## How the Mac app logs (as of owletto `feat/mac-perms-logging`)

`apps/mac/Owletto/Log.swift` — `Log.info/.error/.debug(_ category:, _ message:)`.
Categories: `app`, `sync`, `worker`, `permissions`, `connector`, `runner`, `whatsapp`.

- **os.Logger** under subsystem `ai.lobu.mac`. Interpolations are `privacy: .public`
  — the DEFAULT is `.private`, which renders every value as `<private>`; that alone
  makes a unified-log search look empty while the app is talking normally.
- **File** at `~/Library/Logs/Owletto/owletto.log`, rotating at 5 MB to `.log.1`.
  The file exists because Owletto is `LSUIElement` launched by LaunchServices, so
  `print()`/stdout goes nowhere. Reachable in-app via the "App log" button on the
  error detail (the older "See logs" only appeared for `serverMode == .local`).
- Writes go to a serial background queue. **Never make the logger touch the
  filesystem on the calling thread** — `AppState` is `@MainActor` and a blocking
  `open()` there is the exact bug in [[feedback_never_hot_swap_owletto_app_remotely]].
- `LOBU_OWLETTO_LOG_DIR` redirects the sink; that's how `Tests/LogDedupeTests.swift`
  runs without truncating the user's real log.

**Repeat suppression is keyed per distinct message, NOT per consecutive line.**
The first implementation collapsed only adjacent duplicates and did nothing at
all, because the poll loop emits several different errors per cycle so identical
lines interleave (`A B A B A`). It looked correct in review and was only caught
by reading the produced file back. Mutation-tested: restoring the consecutive-only
logic turns `LogDedupeTests` red.

## Adding a Swift file to the Mac app

`Owletto.xcodeproj` has ONE target and **no** file-system-synchronized groups, so
a new `.swift` file on disk is invisible to the build until it is registered in
four places in `project.pbxproj` (PBXBuildFile, PBXFileReference, the group's
children, the Sources phase) with hand-assigned hex IDs. Symptom is misleading:
only *some* files report `cannot find 'X' in scope` because the compiler bails
mid-batch, which reads as a target-membership problem.

The standalone tests under `apps/mac/Tests/` compile production sources listed in
each file's **header comment**, which `run-tests.sh` executes verbatim. Adding a
new dependency to a production file therefore breaks every test that compiles it
until you add the new source to those headers too — three broke this way here.
Always run the whole suite (`apps/mac/Tests/run-tests.sh`), never just the new test.

fix(mac): one permission per row so expanding cannot move the popover

Expanding the permissions section shifted the whole popover sideways. The
chips were laid out side by side with `.fixedSize(horizontal:)`, so they
refused to compress and the expanded section got a say in the window's
geometry; the popover is anchored under the menu bar icon, so any change
came out as a horizontal jump.

One permission per full-width row, title left and status icon right, through
the same `.menuRow()` styling the context and agent rows already use. A row
ending in `Spacer()` has no intrinsic width to argue with, so the 340pt frame
stays authoritative and expanding can only change height.

Measured on a running build, same session minutes apart:

  before   collapsed  x=1153  340x612     expanded  x=1133  340x629
  after    collapsed  x=1127  340x754     expanded  x=1127  340x862

Note the first theory was wrong and is worth recording: the chips were assumed
to overflow 340pt, but AX reported width pinned at 340 in both states, so a
2/2/1 reflow would have fixed nothing. What actually moved was the popover's
origin. The row layout sidesteps the question rather than tuning widths.

Also drops the chip fill/border entirely and renames chipTooltip to
permissionTooltip, since there are no chips left.

Two of the three are in, building now.

**Permissions count** — `PERMISSIONS 3/5` via a new `badge` slot on the shared header, so it renders in the same position as `CONNECTED AGENTS 5`. It shows in both states rather than only when something's wrong; a badge that appears and disappears is easy to miss.

**Activity indicator** — I went with a **steady dot, not a blink**, and it's worth saying why. A blinking menu bar pulls your eye off whatever you're doing every time a routine sync fires, and it needs a redraw timer to sustain. A dot that's simply present or absent answers "is it doing something right now?" in one glance and costs nothing idle. Easy to change if you'd rather have the pulse.

The harder part was picking the signal. The obvious one, `isSyncing`, is true for a moment on **every poll** — every 10 seconds under computer use — so an indicator bound to it would flicker permanently and mean nothing. I added an `onJobClaimed` callback fired at the point a job is actually claimed, so the dot tracks real work. It also logs `executing <label>`, which the log had no line for.

**Icons — I have not touched yet, and it's a bigger job than it looks.** Confirmed the two brands:

- `public/` was resynced in July (**#536 "sync logos with landing page"**) → red pixel-cross mark
- Mac `AppIcon` + `MenuBarIcon` and all four Chrome extension icons still date from May → orange `< · · >` owl

So both apps genuinely missed that sync. That's **its own PR** — it touches the Chrome extension, which has nothing to do with logging or permissions, and it needs regenerating ten Mac icon sizes plus a monochrome template variant for the menu bar glyph (the menu bar icon must be a template image, so it can't just be a downscale of the colour mark).

I'd rather land #662 first than pile a third concern onto it. Want me to start the icon branch once this builds?

To answer the question directly while that runs: **yes, it has worked** — Behavior 72's previous run `808754` completed cleanly at 17:23 today, so the local CLI does launch and finish e2e. What's broken is narrower and worth separating out:

**The retry ladder has a hole.** After it logs *"leaving the run to the server sweep"* — the correct fail-closed move — a fourth delivery attempt still fires. So the code says it's giving up and then doesn't.

**`round=1` through `round=8` completes in two milliseconds.** That's a resume loop spinning through its entire budget instantly rather than doing work, with `attempt=nil max=nil` where the earlier line had `attempt=2 max=3`. Losing the attempt/max between passes looks like the finalize state isn't surviving.

None of that is caused by tonight's PR — the logging is just the first time any of it has been visible. Previously this failed silently on every launch with nothing written anywhere.

# Pull the swiftc invocation out of the header comment: start at the `swiftc`
# line, keep going while lines continue with a trailing backslash, stop at the
# `&& /tmp/...` run tail.
extract_build_command() {
    awk '
        /^\/\/[[:space:]]*swiftc/ { collecting = 1 }
        collecting {
            line = $0
            sub(/^\/\/[[:space:]]*/, "", line)
            sub(/\\[[:space:]]*$/, "", line)
            printf "%s ", line
            if (line ~ /&&/) exit
            if ($0 !~ /\\[[:space:]]*$/) exit
        }
    ' "$1"
}

passed=0
failed=0
failing_tests=""

for test_file in apps/mac/Tests/*.swift; do
    name="$(basename "$test_file" .swift)"
    if [ -n "$filter" ] && ! echo "$name" | grep -q "$filter"; then
        continue
    fi

    raw="$(extract_build_command "$test_file")"
    if [ -z "$raw" ]; then
        echo "ERROR: $test_file has no 'swiftc' block in its header comment."
        echo "       Add the invocation that builds it so this runner can find it."
        failed=$((failed + 1))
        failing_tests="$failing_tests $name"
        continue
    fi

    # Drop the `&& /tmp/binary` tail — this script runs the binary itself.
    command_head="${raw%%&&*}"

    read -ra tokens <<<"$command_head"
    if [ "${tokens[0]}" != "swiftc" ]; then
        echo "ERROR: $test_file header builds with '${tokens[0]}', not swiftc."

Both fixes are in, on a branch stacked on #662 (kept separate so #662 stays one concern).

## Correction first

My earlier report to you was wrong. **Run 4242 was never wedged.** Every line I read as a production incident came from `DispatcherResumeTests` writing into your real log:

| What I reported | What it actually was |
|---|---|
| Exit report failing 503 → 400 → 502 | Test cases 2, 3, 4 — scripted replies at lines 208/217/228 |
| "Retry ladder has a hole" — delivery after giving up | Case 3 and case 4 are *separate* dispatches, not one ladder |
| "8 rounds in 2ms, resume state lost" | Case 5, which exists to prove the safety cap halts |

Run id 4242 is the fixture's literal id. Those blocks appeared at 00:28/00:56/01:05 because that's when I ran the suite. The retry ladder and resume loop are correct and asserted.

## What was actually broken

**1. The test suite wrote into your production log.** Only `LogDedupeTests` set `LOBU_OWLETTO_LOG_DIR`; every other test that transitively compiles `Log.swift` appended to `~/Library/Logs/Owletto/owletto.log`. The env override can't fix this alone — it only protects tests that remember it, and every test header documents a bare `swiftc` line you can paste without it. So the guard is in the sink: only the app bundle resolves to your log.

Red→green, measured on the real file:
- Pre-fix: log grew **7334 → 7538 bytes** from a test binary, 3 checks failed
- Post-fix: full 11-test suite ran, log stayed **7538 bytes / 02:22**, unchanged

**2. Every Behavior run silently ended the poll drain.** `AppState.swift:1507` folded `connectorKey` into its stop test, but Behavior and device-action runs always return it `nil` — they route by payload, not connector. So a claimed Behavior always hit `break`. A backlog cleared at one job per timer tick: 10 minutes apart whenever computer use is idle.

`git diff --stat feat/mac-perms-logging...HEAD` — 3 files, no strays:
```
 apps/mac/Owletto/AppState.swift            |  29 ++++++---
 apps/mac/Owletto/Log.swift                 |  24 +++++++
 apps/mac/Tests/LogSinkIsolationTests.swift | 101 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
```

## Your e2e question

The CLI path works — run 808754 completed cleanly at 17:23. Run **811959 was never claimed**, and the reason is a stale pin, not the CLI:

- Behavior 72 pins `device_worker_id = e7806c72-…`, whose connections last moved **17:45 yesterday**
- The live worker is `2c295bed-…`, updated **01:09:35 today** (matches this Mac's "executing permissions")

Same stranding as connection 397. The client-side id in UserDefaults (`mac-6e2c3152-…`) is stable, so the churn is server-side worker-row identity, not the app regenerating it.

**Confidence:** Log-sink fix **95** — red/green measured on the real file by byte size, full suite green. Drain fix **75** — reads directly from code and the app builds, but I have not watched two Behaviors drain in one pass live. Stranding diagnosis **85** — from the pin vs. live worker timestamps; I did not read the server's worker-registration code.

**Next actions:**
1. Re-pin Behavior 72 to `2c295bed-…` and re-trigger — that's the actual e2e unblock, and needs a prod write, so say the word.
2. Trace server-side worker-row identity: why one stable client id maps to three rows in two days. That's the root cause behind both the stranded Behavior and connection 397.
3. Push this branch and open it stacked on #662, or fold it in if you'd rather ship one PR.
4. The 21 historical `4242` lines are still in your log — I can trim them or leave as-is.

## What

Two defects in the Mac app, both found while diagnosing what looked like a wedged Behavior run — and the first one is *why* it looked wedged.

### 1. The test suite wrote into the user's production log

`Log.swift`'s file sink accepted any process. Every standalone test under `apps/mac/Tests` that transitively compiles it (`DispatcherResumeTests`, `ExitReportDeliveryTests`, …) appended its **scripted** failures to `~/Library/Logs/Owletto/owletto.log` — the same file the app writes and a human reads when something breaks.

`DispatcherResumeTests` scripts a 503, a 400 and an `<html>502</html>` against run 4242, then drives the local resume cap through 8 rounds. Read back out of the real log, those lines are indistinguishable from a production incident. They cost a full debugging session chasing a wedged Behavior run that never existed, and produced a confident report of three bugs that were all assertions *passing*.

`LOBU_OWLETTO_LOG_DIR` could not fix this alone: it only protects tests that remember to set it, and every test header documents a bare `swiftc` line a human can paste without it. So the guard lives in the sink, where every caller passes regardless of how the binary was launched — only the signed app bundle resolves to the user's log; anything else gets a scratch directory.

### 2. Every Behavior run silently ended the poll drain

The drain loop folded `connectorKey` into its stop test:

```swift
guard result.claimedJob, let key = result.connectorKey, let runId = result.runId else { break }
```

But Behavior runs (`run_type: "behavior"`) and device computer-use actions (`run_type: "action"`) always return it `nil` — they route by payload, not by connector. So a claimed one always hit `break`. A backlog of Behaviors cleared at one job per timer tick, which is **10 minutes** apart whenever computer use is idle.

## Red → green

New `LogSinkIsolationTests` asserts the default path with **no** override set — the configuration that actually broke. Measured against the real file:

**Red** (test compiled against pre-fix `Log.swift` from HEAD):
```
-rw-r--r--  7334 31 Jul 02:20 /Users/burakemre/Library/Logs/Owletto/owletto.log
  ✗ a test binary grew the user's real log by 204 bytes — the sink must refuse it outside the app bundle
  ✗ the probe line reached the user's real log
  ✗ the redirected sink did not receive the line — the guard must redirect the file sink, not disable it
LogSinkIsolationTests: 3 failure(s)
-rw-r--r--  7538 31 Jul 02:22 /Users/burakemre/Library/Logs/Owletto/owletto.log
```

**Green** (post-fix), full suite — including `DispatcherResumeTests`, the worst offender:
```
-rw-r--r--  7538 31 Jul 02:22 owletto.log
LogSinkIsolationTests: all checks passed
-rw-r--r--  7538 31 Jul 02:22 owletto.log     <- unchanged
Swift standalone tests: 11 passed, 0 failed
```

The test asserts on byte *size*, not existence: the user's real log usually does exist, so asserting absence would pass for the wrong reason on a clean machine and fail for a real user. It also asserts the redirected sink **received** the line, so a guard that silently dropped every message can't pass.

## Live e2e

```

11	## The trap: `log` is shadowed in this shell
12	
13	There is a zsh function named `log` on this machine. Every `log show …` invocation
14	hits it, not `/usr/bin/log`, and it fails with:
15	
16	    (eval):log:1: too many arguments
17	
18	With `2>/dev/null` on the command — which is the natural thing to write — this
19	looks like **an empty result set**, not an error. It cost a wrong conclusion
20	("the Mac app emits no logs at all") that survived three separate predicates and
21	got as far as being reported to the user. There were 79,897 lines.
22	
23	**Always use `/usr/bin/log show`, and never suppress stderr on a diagnostic
24	command whose empty output you intend to reason from.** An absence you can't
25	distinguish from an error is not evidence — same family as
26	[[feedback_absence_needs_origin_main_grep]].
27	
28	Useful predicates once you're calling the real binary:
29	
30	    /usr/bin/log show --last 3h --predicate 'process == "Owletto"' --style compact
31	    /usr/bin/log show --last 3h --predicate 'subsystem == "ai.lobu.mac"' --info --debug

33	## How the Mac app logs (as of owletto `feat/mac-perms-logging`)
34	
35	`apps/mac/Owletto/Log.swift` — `Log.info/.error/.debug(_ category:, _ message:)`.
36	Categories: `app`, `sync`, `worker`, `permissions`, `connector`, `runner`, `whatsapp`.
37	
38	- **os.Logger** under subsystem `ai.lobu.mac`. Interpolations are `privacy: .public`
39	  — the DEFAULT is `.private`, which renders every value as `<private>`; that alone
40	  makes a unified-log search look empty while the app is talking normally.
41	- **File** at `~/Library/Logs/Owletto/owletto.log`, rotating at 5 MB to `.log.1`.
42	  The file exists because Owletto is `LSUIElement` launched by LaunchServices, so
43	  `print()`/stdout goes nowhere. Reachable in-app via the "App log" button on the
44	  error detail (the older "See logs" only appeared for `serverMode == .local`).
45	- Writes go to a serial background queue. **Never make the logger touch the
46	  filesystem on the calling thread** — `AppState` is `@MainActor` and a blocking
47	  `open()` there is the exact bug in [[feedback_never_hot_swap_owletto_app_remotely]].
48	- `LOBU_OWLETTO_LOG_DIR` redirects the sink; that's how `Tests/LogDedupeTests.swift`
49	  runs without truncating the user's real log.
50	
51	**Repeat suppression is keyed per distinct message, NOT per consecutive line.**
52	The first implementation collapsed only adjacent duplicates and did nothing at
53	all, because the poll loop emits several different errors per cycle so identical
54	lines interleave (`A B A B A`). It looked correct in review and was only caught
55	by reading the produced file back. Mutation-tested: restoring the consecutive-only
56	logic turns `LogDedupeTests` red.

59	
60	`Owletto.xcodeproj` has ONE target and **no** file-system-synchronized groups, so
61	a new `.swift` file on disk is invisible to the build until it is registered in
62	four places in `project.pbxproj` (PBXBuildFile, PBXFileReference, the group's
63	children, the Sources phase) with hand-assigned hex IDs. Symptom is misleading:
64	only *some* files report `cannot find 'X' in scope` because the compiler bails
65	mid-batch, which reads as a target-membership problem.

67	The standalone tests under `apps/mac/Tests/` compile production sources listed in

69	new dependency to a production file therefore breaks every test that compiles it
70	until you add the new source to those headers too — three broke this way here.
71	Always run the whole suite (`apps/mac/Tests/run-tests.sh`), never just the new test.

---
name: feedback_test_output_in_prod_log_faked_an_incident
description: "I diagnosed and confidently reported three production bugs from log lines that were actually a Swift test's scripted assertions — always establish who WROTE a log line before reasoning from it"
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

Reading `~/Library/Logs/Owletto/owletto.log` I found what looked like a wedged
Behavior run 4242: an exit report failing `503 {"error":"upstream"}` → `400
{"error":"bad request"}` → `<html>502</html>`, a "leaving the run to the server
sweep" line followed by *another* delivery attempt, and a resume loop burning
`round=1 … round=8` in **2 ms** with `attempt=nil max=nil`. I reported all three
to the user as real defects, with a confident causal story for each.

All three were `apps/mac/Tests/DispatcherResumeTests.swift` **passing**. The
503/400/502 are its scripted `Reply` values (cases 2, 3, 4), the two "concurrent"
deliveries are two separate test cases, the 8 instant rounds are case 5 asserting
the local safety cap *halts*, and 4242 is the fixture's literal `run_id`. The
blocks appeared at 00:28/00:56/01:05 because that is when I ran the suite.

The mechanism: every standalone test compiles the production sources it
exercises, several transitively pull in `Log.swift`, and the file sink accepted
any process. Only `LogDedupeTests` set `LOBU_OWLETTO_LOG_DIR`.

**Why:** a log line carries no provenance. "It is in the production log file" felt
like evidence of production behaviour, but the file is just a path any process
can open. Three independent symptoms all reinforcing each other made it feel
*more* confirmed, when in fact they shared a single explanation I had not
considered — correlated evidence is one observation, not three.

**How to apply:**
- Before reasoning from a log line, ask **which process wrote it and when**.
  Cross-check timestamps against what I ran. Here, "these appear only right after
  I run the suite" was visible in the data from the start.
- Treat a fixture-looking id as a fixture until proven otherwise. Prod run ids
  were ~800k; 4242 was three orders of magnitude off and I noticed but explained
  it away as a local-dev DB id instead of grepping the test tree for it.
- Grep the repo for the literal error strings before believing an error is live.
  One `grep -rn '"upstream"' apps/mac/Tests` would have ended this immediately.
- Symptoms that are physically impossible (8 network round-trips + 8 subprocess
  spawns in 2 ms) mean the premise is wrong, not that the bug is exotic. Stop and
  re-derive rather than building a story that accommodates the impossibility.
- Fix belongs at the sink, not the callers: an env override only protects tests
  that remember it, and the test headers document a bare `swiftc` line a human
  can paste without it. Same shape as [[feedback_put_the_check_at_the_chokepoint]].

Related: [[reference_mac_app_logging_and_log_shadowing]] (the other time a
logging artefact produced a confident wrong conclusion — the shadowed `log`
function), [[feedback_stop_when_confidence_diverges]].

## Two fixes

2. **`AppState.swift` poll drain** folded `connectorKey` into its stop test, but
   Behavior (`run_type: "behavior"`) and device action (`run_type: "action"`)
   runs always return it `nil` — they route by payload, not connector. Every
   claimed one hit `break`. Backlogs cleared at one job per timer tick, which is
   **10 minutes** whenever computer use is idle (`feedPollInterval = 600` vs
   `actionPollInterval = 10`). Now `guard result.claimedJob else { break }`, with
   the `recentJobs` recap made conditional.

## Device-worker pinning — NOT a stranding bug

I first read three `device_worker_id`s in `connections` as one Mac churning
identity across relaunches. Wrong. `LobuWorkerIdentity.current()` persists
`lobu.workerId` in UserDefaults and is stable (`mac-6e2c3152-…` here). The rows
are **different machines**:

- `2c295bed-1dfa-4c8b-9f58-c20a62aadfc2` — this MacBook. Owns whatsapp.local,

  which this MacBook never advertises. Quiet since 2026-07-30T17:45.

Tell them apart by which connectors they own, not by recency. Behavior 72 "Device
agy e2e smoke" was pinned to the mini; **I re-pinned it to `2c295bed-…`** via
`client.behaviors.update({ behavior_id, device_worker_id })`. Original value
recorded above — revert by re-pinning to `e7806c72-…`.

A run pinned to an offline device does not hang: run 811959 **failed** after ~65s.

(`~/.local/bin/agy`) spawned on the MacBook, device log line

`query_sql` allowlist, and `behaviors.list` did not return id 72 at all.

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

This is a utilitarian PR deliverable — polished, not flashy.

**Plan** — Color: the subject *is* the brand red `#F5333A`; retired mark's orange `#FF7A18` marks "before"; neutrals biased slightly warm-red rather than pure grey. Type: monospace for the pixel-grid/technical labels (the mark is literally a 20px-cell grid), clean sans for prose. Layout: surface-grouped before/after pairs sitting in checkerboard wells that double as genuine alpha verification.

---
name: reference_owletto_icon_assets_regeneration
description: "Every Owletto icon (Mac AppIcon, menu bar template, Chrome extension) is rendered from public/favicon.svg — the exact rsvg-convert recipe, the two insets, and why the menu bar SVG is hand-maintained"
metadata:
  type: reference
---

Canonical mark: **`public/favicon.svg`** — the Lobu pixel claw, `#F5333A`, a
140×140 viewBox on 20px cells (22 `<rect>`s, 11 per half). `public/icon-512.png`
is its raster. Shipped 2026-07 (#536).

Until owletto #665 (2026-07-31) three surfaces still shipped the **May orange
`<··>` owl**. The full asset list is exactly 15 files — verify with:

    find apps/mac apps/chrome -type f \( -name '*.png' -o -name '*.svg' -o -name '*.icns' \)

## Regenerating the 14 PNGs

    BODY=$(sed -n '/<!-- left half -->/,/<\/svg>/p' public/favicon.svg | sed '$d')
    # Mac:    wrap BODY in <svg viewBox="-20 -20 180 180" fill="#F5333A" shape-rendering="crispEdges">
    # Chrome: wrap BODY in <svg viewBox="-10 -10 160 160" fill="#F5333A" shape-rendering="crispEdges">
    rsvg-convert -w <px> -h <px> -b none <svg> -o <png>

`-b none` is load-bearing — the assets need alpha, not a white square.

Two insets on purpose: **~78% fill** for the macOS app icon (the icon grid
expects breathing room) and **~88%** for Chrome (a 16px toolbar icon needs the
pixels). `AppIcon.appiconset` needs 10 renditions — 16/32/128/256/512 at 1x and
2x, so the 2x file is double the named size (`icon_512x512@2x.png` is 1024px).
Chrome needs 16/32/48/128 per `apps/chrome/manifest.json` (listed twice there:
`icons` and `action.default_icon`).

## The menu bar asset is NOT rendered

`Assets.xcassets/MenuBarIcon.imageset/owletto-mark.svg` is hand-maintained, and
must stay that way: a template image has to be **solid `#000` with its padding
baked into the viewBox** (`-25 -25 190 190`, ~74% fill), because macOS discards
the colour and tints the alpha to the menu bar's light/dark appearance. Its rect
list mirrors `favicon.svg`; keep them in sync by hand. `MenuBarExtra` ignores the
label's frame, so size lives in the asset — `.resizable()`/`.frame()` at the call
site does nothing.

## Verify the built artifact, not the source PNGs

    xcrun assetutil --info <App>.app/Contents/Resources/Assets.car

Should list 10 `AppIcon` renditions plus `MenuBarIcon` at 18 and 36. **`qlmanage
-t` on the .app hangs** (killed at the 2-minute timeout) — do not use it to
render a bundle icon for checking.

Related: [[project_mac_behavior_dispatch_drain]],
[[reference_mac_app_logging_and_log_shadowing]].

14	## Codex quota
15	
16	`make review` (default `REVIEWER_CLI=auto` → codex outside a codex harness) died
17	with `ERROR: You've hit your usage limit … try again at Aug 5th, 2026`. The gate
18	**fails closed on purpose** and will not silently fall back to another reviewer.

20	Switch explicitly: `REVIEWER_CLI=claude CLAUDE_REVIEW_MODEL=fable make review`.
21	`review_validate_claude_model` accepts only `fable`, `opus`, or `claude-opus-*`
22	(`scripts/lib/review-reviewer.sh`) — matching [[feedback_use_fable_for_review]].
23	
24	## The claude reviewer's $schema rejection
25	
26	```
27	Error: --json-schema is not a valid JSON Schema: no schema with key or ref
28	"https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema"
29	```
30	
31	`scripts/review.sh` passes `prompts/review-output-schema.json` verbatim via
32	`--json-schema`, and the Claude CLI's validator does not resolve that meta-schema
33	ref. Nothing to do with the diff under review.
34	
35	Workaround — **working tree only, never commit it** (it belongs in its own PR,
36	not whatever branch you're shipping):
37	
38	```bash
39	cp prompts/review-output-schema.json /tmp/review-schema.bak
40	python3 -c "import json;p='prompts/review-output-schema.json';d=json.load(open(p));d.pop('\$schema',None);json.dump(d,open(p,'w'),indent=2)"
41	REVIEWER_CLI=claude CLAUDE_REVIEW_MODEL=fable make review
42	cp /tmp/review-schema.bak prompts/review-output-schema.json   # restore IMMEDIATELY
43	```
44	
45	Dropping `$schema` removes only the meta-schema declaration; the constraint body
46	is unchanged, so the verdict is still schema-validated. Verify with `git status`
47	after restoring — a stray edit here would land in the next commit.
48	
49	## Re-running review is sometimes mandatory, not a loop
50	
51	`make review` posts `pi-review` against a specific SHA. If anything moves the
52	head — including the Codesmith bot pushing to your open PR branch — the new head
53	has no status and the PR sits `BLOCKED` with nothing explaining why. review.sh
54	detects this and refuses rather than attaching a verdict to a stale commit. That
55	re-run is not the find-fix loop [[feedback_review_is_last_gate_not_the_loop]]
56	warns about.

This is what shows up in package.json files, docs about deployments, the `lobu run` / `lobu apply` CLI surface.
13	
14	- **Owletto** = consumer/personal product. Owns the human-facing apps: macOS menubar app (`Owletto.app`, bundle id `ai.lobu.mac`), Chrome extension, web admin chrome (the popover header reads "Owletto"). This is what end users — including non-developers — see day-to-day.
15

19	
20	**How to apply:** when something is ambiguous, ask which audience it serves. CLI / API / npm / config = Lobu. UI app users click / install / see in System Settings = Owletto. The bridge (e.g. menubar app talking to a `lobu run` server) is fine — Owletto is built ON Lobu, not instead of it. Good catch — and I think you're right, for a reason that's actually in the brand doc I should have checked before building #665.

The split is deliberate: **Lobu = infra/dev surface, Owletto = the consumer app.** Shipping the *identical* Lobu claw on the Mac app and Chrome extension collapses exactly the distinction the two names exist to maintain. I swapped one problem (a stale owl) for another (no differentiation).

The dots are the right vehicle, and the geometry cooperates: at `y=60` the only filled cells are `x=0` and `x=120`, so the whole middle band is free. Dots at `x=40` and `x=80` sit symmetric about the empty centre column — the same eye positions the retired `<··>` owl had.

## Why

#665 replaced the retired owl with the Lobu pixel claw. That fixed the stale mark but introduced a different problem: the Mac app and the Chrome extension then shipped the **identical** Lobu mark.

Lobu and Owletto are deliberately two brands — Lobu is the infra/dev surface (CLI, API, packages), Owletto is the consumer app people install and see in their menu bar. One mark on both collapses exactly the distinction the two names exist to carry. That was my miss in #665, caught on review.

**Side by side, every shipped size:** https://claude.ai/code/artifact/2a1593a3-ef83-40d1-9ebe-9c744fafa180

## What

New source `public/owletto-mark.svg`: the same claw silhouette — Owletto is built *on* Lobu, so the family resemblance is the point — plus two eyes in the centre band.

The eyes are also **continuity**. The mark this line replaced was an owl drawn as `<··>`, and those two dots are the part existing users actually recognise. They read as owl eyes, which is the name.

`public/favicon.svg` is untouched and stays the plain Lobu mark, so the two files sit next to each other and the difference is visible rather than remembered.

## Geometry

The eyes sit **on** the 20px grid at `x=40` and `x=80`, symmetric about the empty centre column that splits the two halves. At `y=60` the only filled cells are `x=0` and `x=120`, so the band was already free — nothing in the claw had to move.

Round dots were tried and rejected: circles fight the pixel idiom and dissolve into mush at 16px, which is exactly the size the Chrome toolbar renders. The 16px pair in the artifact is the comparison that settled it.

## Scope

Owletto-branded app surfaces only — Mac `AppIcon.appiconset` (10 renditions), the menu bar template, and the four Chrome icons. 16 files.

The menu bar SVG stays hand-maintained (a template must be solid `#000` with padding baked into the viewBox) and its comment now points at `owletto-mark.svg` rather than `favicon.svg`, so the next person syncing it copies the right source.

## Open question

`packages/owletto/public/favicon.svg` self-identifies as the **Lobu** mark (`<title>Lobu</title>`) even though it's the web SPA's favicon. I left it alone. If that surface is meant to read as Owletto to end users, it should take the eyes too — say the word and I'll extend this PR.

## Merged

| owletto #662 | `cde8a47a` — logging, collapsible permissions, honest Click & Type |

## What actually happened this session

The through-line worth remembering: I read a wall of `503 / 400 / <html>502</html>` errors in your app log, built a confident three-bug diagnosis from it, and reported it. All of it was `DispatcherResumeTests` **passing** — the test suite was writing its scripted failures into `~/Library/Logs/Owletto/owletto.log`, and run 4242 was a fixture id. That's now fixed at the sink (only the app bundle writes there), with a regression test that measures the real file by byte size.

The second defect was real and independent: every Behavior run silently ended the poll drain, because the stop test required a `connectorKey` that Behavior and action runs never have.

And on your dots question — you caught a genuine miss. #665 fixed a stale mark but made Owletto visually identical to Lobu, collapsing a split the brand doc is explicit about.

## Corrections I made along the way

Three claims of mine turned out wrong and are worth flagging since they shaped earlier answers: there is **no wedged run 4242**; there is **no worker-stranding bug** (three `device_worker_id`s = three machines, distinguishable by which connectors they own, not by recency); and run 811959 didn't hang — it **failed** after ~65s, dispatched to the offline mini.

## Not verified

Menu bar tinting and the Dock icon are asserted from the template contract and the compiled `Assets.car` — never seen in a running installed build. Worth an eyeball on the next real install. Note the Mac app ships via Sparkle, not the prod rollout, so the usual deployed-SHA gate proves nothing here — I didn't set a prod-verify wakeup for that reason.

## Two gate traps, now in memory

`make review-fix` and `make review` are both codex-only and codex is **out of credits until Aug 5**. `REVIEWER_CLI=claude CLAUDE_REVIEW_MODEL=fable` plus the `$schema` workaround is what got through. review-fix's failure is silent — it prints "no summary emitted" and `Error 1`, which reads like "nothing to fix" rather than "the reviewer never ran".

## The bug

#664 added a guard so test binaries stop writing into the user's real log. It compared `Bundle.main.bundleIdentifier` against a hardcoded `"ai.lobu.mac"` — which is the os.Logger **subsystem**, not the bundle id. `PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER` is **`com.owletto.mac`**.

So the comparison was false *for the shipping app*, and it redirected production logs into a per-pid temp directory — silently disabling the exact file the logging work existed to create. No error, no warning; the log just stops.

Caught on a real install, not in review:

```
$TMPDIR/owletto-log-18928/owletto.log
  [app]    launch version=0.1.0 build=1 pid=18928 bundle=/Applications/Owletto.app
  [worker] capabilities=[calendar, computer_use, local_directory, photos, whatsapp_local]
  [worker] executing whatsapp.local

~/Library/Logs/Owletto/owletto.log   <- frozen at the pre-relaunch line
```

## The fix

The test is now **"am I in a bundle at all"**, not "is my id `<literal>`". A standalone `swiftc` executable has no `Info.plist` and therefore a nil `bundleIdentifier` — that's the real distinction being drawn, and it cannot drift when the bundle id is renamed.

## Why the test missed it

This is the part worth reviewing. `LogSinkIsolationTests` could only observe `Bundle.main.bundleIdentifier` of **its own** process, which is always nil. A test binary is *always* the not-an-app case, so it exercised one branch, passed, and reported the guard healthy while the app branch was broken.

The decision is now a pure function taking the identifier as a parameter — not a test-only affordance, but the thing that makes both branches assertable at all. The test drives it with identifiers this process can never have, including **both** `com.owletto.mac` and the `ai.lobu.mac` value that was wrongly treated as authoritative, so reintroducing an equality check against either constant fails.

## Red → green

**Red** — new assertions compiled against the merged `Log.swift` (with a shim mirroring its guard verbatim):

```
✗ a bundled process (com.owletto.mac) must write to /Users/…/Library/Logs/Owletto,
  got /var/folders/…/T/owletto-log-27886
✗ a bundled process (com.example.anything) must write to …
LogSinkIsolationTests: 2 failure(s)
```

**Green** — full suite, and the real log is still untouched by the suite (48 lines before and after):

```
Swift standalone tests: 11 passed, 0 failed
```

## Note

The #664 behaviour this preserves is real and worth keeping: `DispatcherResumeTests` scripts a 503, a 400 and an `<html>502</html>` against run 4242, and those lines landing in `~/Library/Logs/Owletto/owletto.log` cost a full session diagnosing a wedged run that never existed. This fixes the guard's aim, not its purpose.

## Same class, different mechanism: the test could only BE one branch (2026-07-31)

owletto #664 guarded the Mac log sink so test binaries stop writing to the
user's real log, keyed on `Bundle.main.bundleIdentifier`. `LogSinkIsolationTests`
asserted the redirect and passed — but a standalone `swiftc` binary is **always**
the "not an app" case, so it could only ever exercise one branch. The app branch
compared against `"ai.lobu.mac"` (the os.Logger *subsystem*) instead of
`com.owletto.mac`, so the shipping app was misclassified and silently wrote its
logs to a temp dir. Green suite, merged, broken in production; found only by
installing the build and noticing the log had stopped. Fixed in #667.

The skip path here was not a `continue` — it was **the test process's own
identity**, which no assertion could vary. Watch for a guard whose input comes
from ambient process/environment state (`Bundle.main`, `ProcessInfo`, `isatty`,
hostname, platform): the test inherits one value and silently covers half the
decision.

**How to apply:** make the decision a pure function over its inputs and pass them
in, then assert every branch — including values the test process can never have.
Pin the wrong constant too: the fix asserts both `com.owletto.mac` *and*
`ai.lobu.mac`, so reintroducing either equality check fails. Related:
[[project_lobu_owletto_brand_split]] (the two easily-confused identifiers).

content.text: Worth recording — that `appendingPathComponent` trap is subtle and would bite again:

input.old_string: **Repeat suppression is keyed per distinct message, NOT per consecutive line.**
input.new_string:
## `appendingPathComponent` decides trailing slashes by STATTING the disk

Comparing two `URL`s for the same directory is unsafe: `URL` equality treats a
trailing slash as significant, and `appendingPathComponent(_:)` **without** the
`isDirectory:` label determines whether to add one by hitting the filesystem. So
`URL(...).appendingPathComponent("Library/Logs/Owletto")` gains a slash only on a
machine where that directory already exists.

That shipped a test green on this dev box (app installed → directory exists) that
would fail on a fresh CI runner, with **both sides printing the identical path**
in the failure message — maximally confusing. Caught by Codesmith in owletto #668.

**Compare `.path` strings, and always pass `isDirectory:` explicitly.** Applies to
any filesystem URL assertion, not just logging.

**Repeat suppression is keyed per distinct message, NOT per consecutive line.**

## Two mistakes of mine worth naming

Both were in the guard that existed to *prevent* a debugging mistake:

**The bundle-id constant.** I used `"ai.lobu.mac"` — the os.Logger subsystem — where `com.owletto.mac` was needed. That silently sent production logs to a temp dir, and it merged. Found only because you asked whether the logo was on your machine, which made me install a build and notice the log had stopped. If you hadn't asked, it would have sat there until someone next needed a log and found nothing.

**The test comparison.** Codesmith caught that my `URL` equality check depended on `~/Library/Logs/Owletto` already existing, because `appendingPathComponent(_:)` stats the disk to decide on a trailing slash. Green here, would have failed a clean CI runner with both sides printing the same path. I mutation-tested its fix against the original bug — still bites, so it removed the flakiness without weakening the assertion.

The shared root cause is in memory now: a guard whose input comes from ambient process state (`Bundle.main`, `ProcessInfo`) can only ever be one value in a test, so the suite covers half the decision and reports health it hasn't verified. The fix was making the decision a pure function over its inputs.
